paragraphs: §1 — His prophetic claim need not even be investigated; his following is negligible and extinct; and the "unlettered prophet" miracle is no miracle

As for his claim to prophethood and the inquiry into the source of his report (aṣl khabarihi) — we are dispensed from that, since his call (daʿwa) was corrupt. For that is so because every report's source must indeed be inquired into — whether it is true or false — [only] when it is of the kind that reason does not render impossible and that scrutiny (al-naẓar) does not corrupt; but when it is corrupt [and] impossible (fāsidan muḥālan), there is no need to inquire into its source, nor into who transmitted it, and its impossibility and corruption are [themselves] a proof of the mendacity of whoever reports it and whoever transmitted it. Moreover, the source of Abū ʿĪsā's report is too feeble and too flimsy for a doubt to penetrate it or an ambiguity (shubha) to arise within it, since at the outset of his affair only a small band followed him in establishing his prophethood — a band by whose multiples [even] the proof would not be established; and they were, withal, a people barbarous and inarticulate (qawm ʿujm ghutm), deficient in intellects and cognitions (nāqiṣī al-ʿuqūl wa-l-maʿārif). Then they did not cease to dwindle and to die out, until there remained of them but the likeness of twenty or thirty persons at Damascus, and perhaps a small number of them at Isfahan also.

And again: the miracle (muʿjiza) which they claim for him — namely that he was unlettered (ummī) and then brought forth books and scriptures (kutub wa-maṣāḥif) — even were the matter regarding it as they have mentioned, it would have been admissible that he had contrived for that from the outset of his affair and his youth, and feigned ignorance and unletteredness (tazāhara bi-l-jahl wa-l-ummiyya) as a paving-of-the-way (tamhīd) for what was in his soul, and for what he had resolved and determined upon, of claiming prophethood. And this [would hold] if what they said were true — how much the more so when the claim is false!

: A fortiori on the tawātur (mass-transmission) criterion: a report establishes certainty only if transmitted by a multitude too large to have colluded in falsehood; Abū ʿĪsā's original following was so small that "even their multiples" would not reach the threshold at which a claim becomes probative. The same epistemic principle (kull khabar … lā yuḥtaj an yubḥath ʿan aṣlihi) opens Bab 15 against the Christian gospel-report, and Q states it programmatically: a report calling to what reason renders impossible needs no investigation of its chain, because its very impossibility convicts both reporter and transmitter. The argument is the standard kalām treatment of khabar (testimony) and its conditions, here put to anti-messianic use.

: The "unlettered prophet" topos (al-ummī who nonetheless produces kutub wa-maṣāḥif) is borrowed straight from the Islamic iʿjāz tradition — the claim that Muḥammad's illiteracy made the Qurʾān miraculous — and turned against Abū ʿĪsā's followers, who evidently advanced a parallel apologetic for him. Q's reply is the classic deflationary one: prior unletteredness is no miracle, since it could have been feigned (tazāhara) as a long-laid stratagem (tamhīd) — and this concession is granted only arguendo ("even if true"), since Q holds the underlying prophetic claim false outright. Ghutm (s.v. غتم, Lane: barbarousness or impediment of speech, esp. in Arabic; syn. ʿujma) pairs with ʿujm to mark the Isfahani following as a people of foreign, unintelligible speech — Q's contemptuous register for a sect he regards as cognitively negligible (nāqiṣī al-ʿuqūl wa-l-maʿārif).
§2 — Abū ʿĪsā's affirmation of Muḥammad's prophethood is self-refuting on both horns

Then we return to what we mentioned of the corruption of his call and the self-contradiction of his statement, and we say: in his crediting (taṣdīq) of the prophethood of Muḥammad he gives the lie to himself and nullifies what he claimed of prophethood — since Muḥammad had said that there is no prophet after him, and [had thereby] given the lie to Abū ʿĪsā in his claim to prophethood. And [even] were he [Muḥammad] mendacious in his statement that there is no prophet after him — well, a [true] prophet does not lie; and whoever sanctions prophethood for one who lies is [himself] a liar. So mendacity and self-contradiction are necessarily entailed upon Abū ʿĪsā from both directions alike. And I have already composed a book devoted to the invalidation of the prophethood of Muḥammad, and I shall mention something of that hereafter.

: The pivot is Abū ʿĪsā's reported doctrine that Muḥammad (like Jesus before him) was a genuine prophet sent to his own people — a position Q records of the ʿĪsāwiyya in his sectarian survey. Q forges from it a destructive dilemma. If Abū ʿĪsā credits Muḥammad as a true prophet, then he is bound by Muḥammad's own declaration (the khātam al-nabiyyīn doctrine, Q 33:40, "no prophet after him") — which directly falsifies Abū ʿĪsā's own post-Muḥammadan prophetic claim. Taṣdīq (crediting, affirming the truth of) is the technical contrary of takdhīb (giving the lie to): Abū ʿĪsā's taṣdīq of Muḥammad logically commits him to his own takdhīb.

: The second horn closes the dilemma. Suppose instead Muḥammad lied in saying "no prophet after me." Then either (a) a true prophet does not lie — so Muḥammad was no prophet, and Abū ʿĪsā's taṣdīq of him is baseless; or (b) one holds that prophethood may belong to a liar — but then "whoever sanctions prophethood for a liar is himself a liar," so Abū ʿĪsā is again convicted. Either way al-kadhib wa-l-munāqaḍa (mendacity and self-contradiction) are "entailed from both directions" (min al-jihatayn jamīʿan) — Q's recurring formula for an opponent impaled on both horns (cf. the Christological dilemmas of Babs 2 and 6). The promised "book devoted to the invalidation of the prophethood of Muḥammad" is the anti-Islamic treatise Q announces again at the head of Bab 15 (allaftu fī dhālika kitāban mufradan); whether it was a separate work or a lost section of the Anwār is uncertain. The "hereafter" (fīmā baʿd) points forward to Bab 15, the refutation of Islam and of all who affirm the prophethood of the Messiah.

- The bab's subject and adversary. The heading reads fī al-radd ʿalā ilḥādatihi al-maʿrūf bi-Abī ʿĪsā al-Iṣbahānī — "on the refutation of his heresy, [that of] the one known as Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣbahānī." (Ilḥāda, abstract noun of ilḥād, "apostasy/heresy"; Q classes the pseudo-messianic claimant among the mulḥidūn.) The target is Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣbahānī, the Persian-Jewish pseudo-messiah of the early Islamic period (Umayyad/early ʿAbbāsid), founder of the ʿĪsāwiyya sect. Q treats him at greater length in the heresiography of Maqala I; here, in the Christological-and-prophetological block of Maqala III, he is dispatched in two compact sections because the case is, in Q's view, beneath sustained argument. Note the placement: between the refutation of Christian Christology (Babs 1–12) and the long refutation of naskh (abrogation, Bab 14) and of Islam and the Christian Messiah (Bab 15), Abū ʿĪsā is the intra-Jewish false-prophet case in the prophetological sequence.

- The two-pronged structure. §1 is epistemological-and-sociological: the claim is so manifestly impossible that it needs no inquiry into its chain of transmission (the kalām khabar-criterion), and in any case its following was always negligible and is now all but extinct (twenty or thirty at Damascus, a handful at Isfahan). §2 is the logical coup: Abū ʿĪsā's own taṣdīq of Muḥammad's prophethood is self-refuting on both horns of the disjunction (Muḥammad spoke truly → no prophet after him → Abū ʿĪsā disqualified; Muḥammad lied → a liar is no prophet, or one who licenses a lying prophet is himself a liar → Abū ʿĪsā disqualified). This min al-jihatayn jamīʿan ("from both directions alike") dilemma-form is Q's signature destructive move throughout the Maqala.

- The "unlettered prophet" miracle. §1's deflation of the ummī miracle is pointed: the very topos the Muslim iʿjāz tradition applied to Muḥammad (an illiterate man producing Scripture) was evidently transferred by the ʿĪsāwiyya to Abū ʿĪsā. Q neutralizes it with the tamhīd (long-laid-stratagem) reply — feigned illiteracy proves nothing — and grants it only arguendo, since he denies the prophetic claim outright. The same logic implicitly cuts against the Islamic version, anticipating the anti-Islamic argument of Bab 15.

- Cross-references to a separate anti-Islamic book. Q twice announces a kitāb mufrad devoted to invalidating Muḥammad's prophethood — here at §2 ("I have already composed a book … and I shall mention something of that hereafter") and again at the head of Bab 15. This is one of several places where Q defers full treatment of a topic to a dedicated work; the relationship of that work to the Anwār and to his Torah-commentary (the Kitāb al-Riyāḍ wa-l-Ḥadāʾiq) is not certain.

- For Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣbahānī and the ʿĪsāwiyya: Q's own heresiographical account in Kitāb al-Anwār Maqala I (Nemoy, "Al-Qirqisānī's Account of the Jewish Sects," HUCA 7 (1930), 317–397, at the ʿĪsāwiyya section); Steven M. Wasserstrom, "The ʿĪsāwiyya Revisited," Studia Islamica 75 (1992); and the classic treatments in Israel Friedlaender, "Jewish-Arabic Studies: Shiitic Influences in Jewish Sectarianism," JQR 1–3 (1910–1913). For the historical and chronological problems of dating Abū ʿĪsā (Umayyad vs. early ʿAbbāsid), see Wasserstrom and the entry in the Encyclopaedia Judaica, s.v. "Abu ʿIsa al-Isfahani."

- For the khabar / tawātur (mass-transmission) criterion invoked in §1: the standard Bahshamī treatment of testimony and the conditions under which khabar yields knowledge — ʿAbd al-Jabbār, al-Mughnī vol. 15 (al-Tanabbuʾāt wa-l-Muʿjizāt), and Sharḥ al-Uṣūl al-Khamsa on al-akhbār; Q reproduces the principle (a report calling to the rationally impossible needs no chain-investigation) verbatim at the head of Bab 15. See glossary §VII (prophetology / muʿjiza anchor terms, to be filled as M3 B15–16 are translated).

- For the khātam al-nabiyyīn doctrine Q exploits in §2: Qurʾān 33:40 (mā kāna Muḥammad … wa-lākin rasūl Allāh wa-khātam al-nabiyyīn), the "seal of the prophets" verse underwriting the claim that there is no prophet after Muḥammad — the premise of Q's first horn.

- For the promised anti-Islamic treatise (kitāb mufrad fī ifsād nubuwwat Muḥammad): the matching announcement at the head of Bab 15; on Q's lost or embedded polemical works, Bruno Chiesa and Wilfrid Lockwood, Yaʿqūb al-Qirqisānī on Jewish Sects and Christianity (1984), and Georges Vajda's studies of the Anwār's anti-Christian and anti-Muslim sections.
